No special foam. They drench them in a factory oil that protects them during storage. Step one for new guns is to clean off that factory oil with solvent and then lube them properly.

Go to a furniture store, or find somebody who just bought some new furniture, or just bite the bullet and freaking buy a hand sized desiccant packet. Toss it underneath the foam in your case. Moisture solved - especially if you got a watertight pelican.

Gun cleaning is easy.

Follow the instructions in the manual for breaking it down. Wipe the gunk off all the parts, using a rag (or paper towels) and some sort of gun solvent. Hoppes is fine. Pay attention to the breech face, the slide rails, and the little area under the extractor.

It does not have to be spotless, just smooth.

After cleaning comes oiling. Any ordinary gun oil is fine - Hoppes makes a nice gun oil in an orange bottle, it's just mineral oil, same as cutting board oil. I use it for everything. Avoid 3M and WD40, they turn to varnish as they age. Put some oil on a clean rag, wipe all the parts smooth with it, it leave behind a thin film to prevent rust. Follow the lube instructions in the manual, but it usually means a drop on each slide rail, and a little dab wherever you see a shiny spot forming.

You can use grease for lube if you want, too. I have a container of purple synthetic stuff I got for my motorbike and it's amazing, and that tube will last twenty lifetimes.

Cleaning the bore is not terribly important, but cleaning the chamber is. Use the brush as a chamber brush, put it in a little and spin it in a circle. Then push it out the front and you're done brushing. Push a wad of oiled patch through and you're finished. There is no point in scrubbing the bore clean, the fouling is self-limiting and it returns after the next shot anyway. So long as it is oiled it won't rust.

One more thing you need is a holster. Get in the habit of the gun not being in your hands unless you are bringing it up to aim. If you are just holding it, put in in the holster. Develop a holy and iron habit of inserting the gun into the holster only, and forever only, when your trigger finger is straight. I like to touch the edge of the holster with the tip of my trigger finger before sliding it in, and I won't do it without that touch first.

I had a snake originally for the smaller form factor in drastically lower cost. Two uses was all it took to convince me to go and buy a real cleaning rod.

You clean parts with the solvent, heat the parts with a blow dryer and apply the paste. Keep heating it until it melts to a liquid and wipe everything completely DRY. This is a dry lube that permeates metal and won't collect dust, leaving it wet will cause you problems. If you follow these steps the only cleaning you need is a wipe down with a clean microfiber after shooting.
